docs.title: A first-run account of NVIDIA NIM hosted endpoints
docs.text: This is my experience visiting build.nvidia.com create an account, get an API key, and query a NIM hosted endpoint to get a model response. This is my attempt to understand the developer journey starting from built.nvidia.com to getting my first model response using a NVIDIA NIM hosted endpoint.

docs.title: How long it took
docs.text:
I went from zero to a working API key in about 3 minutes. The account creation, sign-in, and phone verification all fit inside that window without much friction once the right button was found.

It took another three minutes to create a script and get a first model response. The longest wait in the entire session wasn't signup or key generation it was the model's own first response, which took up to a couple of minutes to complete

docs.title: What's here
docs.text:
• Getting access — the account and key flow
  • First call — how I got to a working response, and what to expect while waiting
  • The example scripts- an explanation of two script and what each one is for

docs.title: The example scripts
docs.text:
Two small scripts, both calling the same model (moonshotai/kimi-k3) on the same endpoint, https://integrate.api.nvidia.com/v1. I created both scripts to demonstrate how to get a raw response directly from a NIM endpoint. The second script uses the OpenAI SDK to see if we can easily swap in different models at will.

uv run python examples/nim-example-openai.py
uv run python examples/nim-example-nvidia.py

docs.title: nim-example-nvidia.py — raw requests
docs.text:
Calls the endpoint directly with requests, stream=True, and prints each server-sent event line as-is: data: {...} chunks, exactly as they come off the wire. Nothing is parsed. This is the shape the catalog's own Shell example gives you, made a little more durable (explicit timeout, real error handling).

It sends a multimodal request — text plus an image URL — to Kimi-K3, and got a real response when run.

Reach for this version when you want to see the raw protocol, or you're debugging something a parsed client might be hiding from you.

docs.title: nim-example-openai.py — OpenAI-compatible client
docs.text:
Points the OpenAI SDK at base_url="https://integrate.api.nvidia.com/v1" instead of OpenAI's own endpoint. This works, but it's not something the catalog UI confirmed directly: the model page's Python tab only offered a raw requests snippet, with no OpenAI-client option shown.

This script also parses the streamed chunks into delta objects and measures time-to-first-token, printed at the end of the run.

docs.title: The reasoning_content extension
docs.text:
Captured chunks (examples/example.json, examples/example-nv.json, both captured from this endpoint's own streaming output, since the API reference had no response example) show the ordering: early chunks carry delta.reasoning_content, then the delta switches to delta.content once the actual answer starts. For example:

{"delta": {"role": "assistant", "reasoning_content": " user"}, ...}

followed later by chunks like:

{"delta": {"content": "ential", ...}, ...}

reasoning_content is a NIM extension — it isn't part of the OpenAI chat-completions schema. The script handles this by checking content first and falling back to reasoning_content.

The API reference's built-in try-it tool (on docs.api.nvidia.com) was the first thing tried to inspect a response shape, but it failed repeatedly in Chrome with a bearer token pasted in:

Network Error: The request could not be completed. This is typically caused by a
CORS issue, a network error, or an invalid URL.

docs.title: Why the timeout is explicit
docs.text: Both scripts set an 180s read timeout rather than relying on the client default (600s for the OpenAI SDK). Given first-token times observed in the 33-70s range, a 600s default is too long to catch a genuine stall.

docs.title: First call
docs.text: Going from a working API key to a real model response.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. From the model's catalog page, select the Shell tab.
  2. Copy the prefilled command shown there and run it. The key is already filled in.

docs.title: Set your expectations on timing
docs.text:
The catalog's prefilled example ships with reasoning_effort set to max. At that setting, expect:

  • ~30-70 seconds before the first token appears
  • A couple of minutes total before the response finishes

The response does stream — it isn't silent for the whole wait — but the gap before anything shows up is long enough to wonder if the request is stuck. It isn't; that's the normal range observed here.

docs.title: About reasoning_effort
docs.text:
This parameter is documented in the API reference and controls how much reasoning the model does before answering. It's tempting to lower it to speed things up.

Worth knowing before you do the same: across single runs at low, high, and max, first-token time ranged from about 33s to about 71s, and the two low runs alone differed by nearly 2x. Lowering reasoning_effort did not reliably reduce the wait in these runs. Run-to-run variance looked larger than any difference between settings. This isn't a controlled benchmark, so treat it as one data point. Bottom line is don't count on this parameter to reduce the take it takes to get the first token.

See the example scripts for a script that measures time-to-first-token directly.

docs.title: Getting access
docs.text: This is the path from a cold start (no account, no key) to a working API key, as it actually happened. Total elapsed time: about 3 minutes.

docs.title: What worked well
docs.text:
• Getting started was easy Just sign up for an account, pick a model, copy a code snippet from the model page, and run it
  • No other accounts needed The whole flow stayed on build.nvidia.com.
  • The code samples come with the API key already filled in once you have one. That made the first call easy. No separate step to wire the key into the example.

docs.title: The path
docs.text:
1. Start at build.nvidia.com.
  2. Click a model in the catalog — in this case the first one listed, Kimi-K3 (moonshotai/kimi-k3).
  3. Click Generate API Key. This prompts a sign-in.
  4. The sign-in screen is also the signup route — it just doesn't say so. Signing in is obvious; signing up isn't a separate, labeled option. The fastest way through is a social login (Google, in this case): choosing it creates the account implicitly, with no separate signup step. Knowing that going in saves the minute or so otherwise spent looking for a "create account" link.
  5. Verify by phone (SMS code) when prompted.
  6. Back on the model page, select the Shell tab and click Generate API Key again to get a key tied to your account.
